content: Elective hysterectomy is a common surgical procedure performed for benign gynecological conditions. This surgery can be conducted through abdominal, laparoscopic, or vaginal approaches, with or without laparoscopic assistance. Antibiotic prophylaxis involves administering antibiotics to reduce the risk of postoperative infections, which can affect 40% to 50% of women undergoing vaginal hysterectomy and over 20% of those undergoing abdominal hysterectomy. Despite the clinical importance of this topic, no prior Cochrane review has systematically evaluated the evidence regarding the effectiveness and safety of antibiotic prophylaxis in this context. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of antibiotic prophylaxis in women undergoing elective hysterectomy. A comprehensive search of electronic databases was conducted up to November 2016, including sources such as the Cochrane Gynaecology and Fertility Group Specialised Register, Cochrane Central Register of Studies, MEDLINE, Embase, PsycINFO, and CINAHL, as well as clinical trial registries, conference abstracts, and reference lists of relevant articles. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing antibiotics to placebo or other antibiotics as prophylaxis in women undergoing elective hysterectomy. Standard Cochrane methodological procedures were employed for data collection and analysis. A total of 37 RCTs involving 6079 women were included in the review, encompassing 20 comparisons of various antibiotics versus placebo and versus one another. The quality of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, with limitations including risk of bias due to poor reporting of methods, imprecision from small sample sizes and low event rates, and inadequate reporting of adverse effects. For vaginal hysterectomy, low-quality evidence indicated that antibiotic prophylaxis significantly reduced the risk of total postoperative infections (risk ratio [RR] 0.28, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.19 to 0.40), urinary tract infections (UTIs) (RR 0.58, 95% CI 0.43 to 0.77), pelvic infections (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.20 to 0.39), and postoperative fevers (RR 0.43, 95% CI 0.34 to 0.54). These findings suggest that antibiotic prophylaxis decreases the average risk of postoperative infection from approximately 34% to between 7% and 14%. However, the impact on rates of other serious infections remains unclear (RR 0.20, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.10), and data on adverse effects were insufficient. For abdominal hysterectomy, women receiving antibiotic prophylaxis experienced fewer total postoperative infections (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.21 to 0.67), abdominal wound infections (RR 0.51, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.73), UTIs (RR 0.41, 95% CI 0.31 to 0.53), pelvic infections (RR 0.50, 95% CI 0.35 to 0.71), and postoperative fevers (RR 0.59, 95% CI 0.50 to 0.70). These results suggest that antibiotic prophylaxis reduces the average risk of postoperative infection from approximately 16% to between 1% and 6%. The effect on rates of other serious infections remains uncertain (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.12 to 1.69), and it is unclear whether adverse effects differed between groups (RR 1.80, 95% CI 0.62 to 5.18). Head-to-head comparisons of different antibiotics for vaginal hysterectomy included cephalosporins versus penicillin, cephalosporins versus tetracycline, antiprotozoals versus lincosamides, and cephalosporins versus antiprotozoals. No significant differences were observed for most primary outcomes, except that cephalosporins were associated with fewer total postoperative infections and postoperative fevers compared to antiprotozoals. Adverse effects were reported in only one comparison (cephalosporins vs penicillin), with no differences between groups. For abdominal hysterectomy, only one comparison (cephalosporins vs penicillin) was identified, and no significant differences were observed for primary outcomes. Adverse effects were not reported. Comparisons of combined antibiotics versus single antibiotics for vaginal hysterectomy included cephalosporin plus antiprotozoal versus cephalosporin, cephalosporin plus antiprotozoal versus antiprotozoal, and penicillin plus antiprotozoal versus penicillin. Data were unavailable for most outcomes, including adverse effects. However, fewer women receiving cephalosporin with antiprotozoal experienced total postoperative infections, UTIs, or postoperative fevers compared to those receiving antiprotozoal alone. For abdominal hysterectomy, one comparison (penicillin plus antiprotozoal vs penicillin alone) was identified, but differences between groups were unclear, and adverse effects were not reported. Single small trials addressed dose comparisons of cephalosporins, but no data were available for most outcomes, including adverse effects. No trials compared different routes of administration. The quality of evidence for all head-to-head and dose comparisons was very low due to serious imprecision and risk of bias from poor reporting of methods. In conclusion, antibiotic prophylaxis appears to be effective in reducing postoperative infections in women undergoing elective vaginal or abdominal hysterectomy, regardless of the dose regimen. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether prophylactic antibiotics influence rates of adverse effects or to identify the safest and most effective antibiotic, dose regimen, or route of administration. Additionally, the most recent studies included in this review were 14 years old at the time of the search, raising concerns about the applicability of findings to current perioperative and postoperative care practices and antimicrobial resistance patterns.
